title: bitwise operators
concept: Bitwise operators manipulate integers in binary bit units and are key for flag management and optimization.

steps.title: Include stdio.h header
steps.explanation:
Include standard input/output headers with **`#include <stdio.h>`** for use with `printf`.

In this lesson, you will learn **Bit Operators**, which directly manipulate **Bits**, the most basic data unit of a computer.

steps.title: Start main function
steps.explanation:
**`int main()`** --- The starting point of the program, the main stack frame is created.

Bit operations are the lowest-level operations that computers use to process data.

steps.title: Initializing variable with binary number
steps.explanation: **`unsigned char a = 0b11001010;`**, **`unsigned char b = 0b10110101;`** --- The `0b` prefix means **binary literal**. `unsigned char` is **an unsigned 8-bit integer** (0 to 255).

steps.title: AND operation (&) - 1 if both are 1
steps.explanation: **`a & b`** --- The **AND operation** results in 1 only** when both bits are **1. `a: 11001010`, `b: 10110101` -> `a&b: 10000000` = **128**.

steps.title: OR operation (|) - 1 if at least one is 1
steps.explanation: **`a | b`** --- **OR operation** results in 1 if **any one of the two bits** is 1. `a: 11001010`, `b: 10110101` -> `a|b: 11111111` = **255**.

steps.title: XOR operation (^) - 1 if different
steps.explanation: **`a ^ b`** --- **XOR (eXclusive OR) operation** is 1 when two bits are **different**, and 0 if they are the same. `a: 11001010`, `b: 10110101` -> `a^b: 01111111` = **127**.

steps.title: NOT operation (~) - bit inversion
steps.explanation: **`(unsigned char)~a`** --- The **NOT operation** inverts all bits. `a: 11001010` -> `~a: 00110101` = **53**.

steps.title: Reset bit flags
steps.explanation: **`int flags = 0;`** --- Now let's look at **Bit Flags**, which are practical uses of bit operations. Initializing `flags` to 0 turns off all 32 bits.

steps.title: Turn on specific bits with left shift
steps.explanation: **`flags |= (1 << 2);`** --- This is a command to “turn on bit 2”. If you move `00000001` 2 places to the left with `1 << 2`, it becomes `00000100` (=4), and if you OR assign it with `flags |= 4`, it becomes `00000000 | 00000100 = 00000100`.

steps.title: Bit setting confirmation output
steps.explanation: **`printf("Set bit 2: %d\n", flags);`** --- `flags` value `4` is printed. In the binary number `00000100`, only bit 2 (third from the right) is on.

steps.title: Check specific bits with right shift
steps.explanation: **`(flags >> 2) & 1`** --- This is a practical pattern that **Checks** whether a specific bit is turned on. Move the bit to the right 2 places with `flags >> 2` (`00000100`->`00000001`) to move the bit you want to check to position 0, and extract only the last bit with `& 1`.

a | b = 255
a ^ b = 127
~a = 53

steps.title: Program exit
steps.explanation:
**`return 0;`** --- The program terminates normally, and all local variables are returned from memory along with the main stack frame being released.

misconceptions.wrong: Bit operations are used only in system programming.
misconceptions.correct: Bitwise operations are used in a variety of fields, including permission management, network protocols, game state management, and graphics.
misconceptions.why: This is because a single integer can efficiently manage multiple states, providing both memory and speed advantages.

keyTakeaway: Bitwise operations (&, |, ^, ~, <<, >>) directly manipulate integers in binary bit units and are key to flag management and performance optimization.
